11520:
Imagine a vast layer of rock sitting underground. Now imagine that layer being pushed upward — or the soil around it being worn away by rain and wind over thousands of years — until a portion of that rock breaks through the surface and becomes visible. That exposed, protruding portion of rock is called an outcropping.

In the simplest terms: an outcropping is a mass of rock that sticks up or out from the surrounding ground or hillside, like the tip of something much larger hiding beneath.

Think of a grassy hillside. Most of the hill is covered with soil, grass, and trees. But in one spot, a jagged chunk of dark grey rock juts out of the slope — rough, exposed, bare. That's an outcropping.

Or think of a desert landscape where you see enormous flat-topped rock formations rising dramatically from the sandy ground, with their lower layers buried but their upper portions sticking out boldly. Those are outcroppings.

The key visual idea is always something beneath the surface breaking through and becoming visible above it.

Two main things cause outcroppings to form:

  1. Erosion — Rain, rivers, and wind gradually strip away the soil and softer material on top, slowly revealing the harder rock underneath. Since rock is much tougher than soil, it survives the erosion while everything around it gets worn down.
  2. Geological pressure — Deep underground forces push rock layers upward over millions of years until they poke through the surface.
How is it different from just "a rock"?

A rock sitting on the ground is simply a loose rock. An outcropping is connected to the bedrock beneath — it is part of a continuous underground rock layer or mass. It is not a separate object; it is the visible part of something much bigger that is mostly hidden underground. This is an important distinction.

The word is most commonly used in:

  • Geology and earth science — Scientists study outcroppings to understand what types of rock exist underground without having to dig.
  • Hiking, mountaineering, and nature writing — Describing rocky terrain, cliff faces, and mountain landscapes.
  • Mining and oil exploration — Outcroppings can reveal what minerals or resources might lie deeper underground.
  • Architecture and landscaping — Rock outcroppings are sometimes incorporated into garden designs or building sites.

Like many concrete words in English, "outcropping" is also used figuratively — that is, metaphorically — to describe anything that is a visible sign or small emergence of something larger and mostly hidden.

For example:

  • "The argument was just an outcropping of deeper resentments that had been building for years."
    Here, the argument is like the exposed rock — the visible part of a much bigger, hidden problem below the surface.
  • "Small outcroppings of resistance began to appear across the country."
    Meaning: small, visible signs of a broader, underlying resistance that was growing.

The figurative sense always preserves the same logic: a small, visible portion of something that is much larger and mostly unseen or hidden beneath the surface.

You will often see both "outcropping" and "outcrop" used to mean the same thing. Outcrop is slightly more common in strict geological writing, while outcropping tends to appear more in everyday and literary contexts. Treat them as interchangeable — they refer to the same thing.

• The geologist examined the limestone outcropping on the side of the canyon.
  • Hikers rested on a flat granite outcropping that offered a clear view of the valley.
  • The construction crew had to blast through a large outcropping before they could lay the road.
  • Her brief smile was a small outcropping of the warmth she rarely showed anyone.

An outcropping is a mass of rock that has broken through the earth's surface and is now visibly sticking out from the surrounding ground — the exposed, protruding face of an otherwise buried rock layer — and by extension, any small, visible sign of a larger hidden thing.
11521: An outcry is a strong, loud expression of anger, protest, or shock — usually from many people at once — in reaction to something that feels wrong, unfair, or deeply troubling. Think of it as the collective voice of people who are upset and want to be heard.
The Two Senses of the Word

Outcry has two senses: one literal and one figurative. The figurative one is by far the more common in modern English.

The literal sense means an actual, audible cry — a shout of alarm, pain, or shock. For example: "There was an outcry from the stadium crowd when the goalkeeper was knocked unconscious." Here, people are physically crying out. This sense is older and less frequently used today.

The figurative sense — the one you will encounter most often — refers to a wave of strong public reaction against something. It doesn't involve actual screaming, but the emotion is just as intense. It is the kind of reaction where many people, together, express their anger or disapproval loudly and persistently. For example: "The government's decision to cut hospital funding sparked a nationwide outcry." Nobody is literally shouting, but the public is making a lot of noise through protests, social media, petitions, speeches, interviews, and demonstrations.
What Makes Something an "Outcry" and Not Just Criticism

This is important. Not every complaint or disagreement is an outcry. The word carries specific qualities that set it apart:

It is intense. An outcry is not mild displeasure or a quiet frown of disapproval. It is fuelled by strong emotion — outrage, indignation, moral shock. When people feel something is deeply wrong or unjust, that is when an outcry happens.

It is usually collective. A single person complaining is not an outcry. The word strongly suggests a group — often a large group — reacting together. This is why you will so often see it paired with the word "public," as in "public outcry." That phrase means that ordinary people, broadly and widely, are expressing strong disapproval.

It is reactive. An outcry doesn't appear out of nowhere. Something triggers it — a decision, an event, a revelation, a scandal, an injustice. The outcry is the response to that trigger.

It implies the reaction is justified, or at least understandable. When a writer uses the word "outcry," there is usually a quiet suggestion that the people reacting have a good reason to be upset. It gives the protest a sense of legitimacy.
How the Word Is Actually Used

Knowing how "outcry" is used in real sentences is just as important as knowing the definition. Here are the patterns you'll most commonly see:

"Public outcry" is the most frequent combination. "The new law caused a public outcry." The word "public" tells you the anger is widespread, not limited to one group.

"Widespread outcry" is similar. It emphasizes that the reaction extends across many different places or communities.

Outcry is often "caused," "sparked," "triggered," or "provoked" by something. These verbs all point to the idea that an event sets it off. "The CEO's pay raise sparked an outcry among employees."

Outcry can also be described as happening "amid" or "in the face of" something. "The company proceeded with its plans amid widespread outcry." This means the company ignored the protest and moved ahead anyway.

Outcry is very often followed by "over" or "against." "There was an outcry over the proposed demolition of the historic building." / "An outcry against the new tax policy grew louder each day."
Concrete Examples to Cement Your Understanding

Imagine a beloved park in a city is going to be torn down to build a parking lot. Residents, environmentalists, and local historians are furious. They write letters, hold protests, post on social media, and appear on the news demanding the plan be stopped. This collective anger and protest is an outcry — specifically, a public outcry against the destruction of the park.

Imagine a famous athlete is caught cheating in a competition. Fans, sports commentators, fellow athletes, and the media are all reacting with disbelief and anger. The reaction that follows — the flood of angry opinions, the demand for consequences, the sense of moral betrayal felt by millions — is an outcry.

Now imagine a quieter scenario: a child stumbles and falls at a playground. Another child nearby lets out a gasp and cries out in alarm. That sudden, audible cry is also an outcry — in its more literal, physical sense.

When you read or hear the word "outcry," it should immediately signal to you that something significant has happened and people are not staying quiet about it. It carries a sense of urgency, of moral weight, of people who feel they cannot and will not stay silent. It is a word associated with justice, protest, and collective conscience. It is rarely used for trivial things. When something provokes an outcry, it means it has genuinely disturbed or angered a large number of people.

Complaint is calm and formal. You file a complaint. An outcry is emotional and urgent — you don't file an outcry, you cause one or spark one.

Protest is close in meaning, but a protest is often a planned, organized action (like a march or demonstration). An outcry can be spontaneous and unorganized — it is the raw reaction before any formal protest is even planned.

Uproar and furore are very close synonyms. The slight difference is that "outcry" often emphasizes the sense of moral outrage and the voices of real people, while "uproar" emphasizes the chaotic noise and disorder, and "furore" is often used for short-lived but intense media or public controversy.

Criticism is intellectual and measured. An outcry is emotional and collective. You can criticize something calmly and alone; an outcry requires intensity and usually numbers.

"Outcry" is a neutral-to-formal word. It fits naturally in news reporting, academic writing, formal essays, and serious conversation. It is not slang, and it is not overly technical. You will regularly see it in newspapers, political discussions, social commentary, and literature.

If you had to capture everything above in one sentence, it would be this: an outcry is a strong, emotional reaction — usually of anger or protest — from many people together, triggered by something they feel is wrong, unfair, or shocking, expressed so loudly and persistently that it cannot be ignored.
11522:
Something is outdated when it was once current, useful, or accepted — but is no longer so, because the world has moved on. It belongs to a past moment that has now been replaced by something newer, more accurate, or more suitable.

The key idea is a mismatch with the present. The thing itself hasn't necessarily broken or disappeared — it just no longer fits now.

Think of it this way: "outdated" is built from the idea of being past its date — like a deadline that's already passed. Something outdated has, in a sense, expired its relevance.

It always implies a comparison between then (when it was fine) and now (when it isn't). Without that contrast, the word doesn't apply.
What Kinds of Things Can Be Outdated?

Almost anything can be outdated — and understanding this range is essential:

Information and knowledge
If a textbook says the population of a country is 80 million, but the actual population is now 130 million, that information is outdated. It was once correct. Now it misleads.

Technology
A floppy disk is outdated. It was once the standard way to store and transfer files. Computers no longer even have slots for them. Using one today is impractical — not because it's broken, but because the world has moved to USB drives, cloud storage, and beyond.

Methods and practices
Doctors once used to bleed patients (literally cut them and drain blood) to cure illness. That method is outdated — completely replaced by better medical understanding.

Laws and rules
Some countries still have laws on their books that were written centuries ago. Those laws may be outdated — written for a reality that no longer exists.

Ideas and beliefs
The idea that the Earth is the centre of the universe was once widely believed. It is now an outdated belief — overturned by science.

Design and style
A website built in the late 1990s — with flashing text, tiled backgrounds, and giant buttons — looks visually outdated today, because design standards have evolved completely.

Software
If you're running an old version of an app that no longer receives updates, it is outdated — it may have security vulnerabilities, missing features, and poor compatibility with modern systems.
The Spectrum: How "Outdated" Relates to Other Words

This is crucial for a learner. Several words sit near "outdated," but they are not identical.

Old is neutral. A 100-year-old painting is old, but it isn't outdated — it wasn't made to be "current." "Old" simply describes age.

Outdated carries a sense of failure to keep up. It implies something should be current or was once current, but has fallen behind.

Obsolete is stronger than outdated. When something is obsolete, it is not just behind — it is completely out of use. No one uses it anymore. The VCR is arguably obsolete. An outdated thing can often still be used (awkwardly or poorly); an obsolete thing typically cannot be used at all in practical terms.

Old-fashioned tends to be used more for style, attitude, or social customs — and often carries a warmer or more nostalgic tone. "He has old-fashioned manners" is not a harsh criticism. "Outdated" is more neutral-to-negative, and more commonly applied to facts, systems, and technology.

Stale is used specifically for information or content that was once fresh and current but has gone dry — like stale news or stale data.

"Outdated" is mildly negative, but not harshly so. It doesn't insult — it simply identifies a gap between what is and what should be for the present time.

When someone says your thinking is outdated, they mean your ideas haven't kept pace with what is now known or accepted. It's a criticism, but a factual one rather than a personal attack.

When you say a machine is outdated, you're saying: it works, perhaps, but it's no longer the right tool for today's world.

"Outdated" sits comfortably in two positions in a sentence:

Before the noun (attributive position):
"This is an outdated map."
"We're using outdated equipment."

After a linking verb (predicative position):
"This map is outdated."
"The equipment feels outdated."
"The policy has become outdated."

Both are natural and common. The word works smoothly in either place.

Certain words pair with "outdated" so often that knowing them will help you recognise and use the word naturally:

  • outdated information / data / statistics — facts that are no longer current
  • outdated technology / software / hardware / systems — tools that have been surpassed
  • outdated methods / practices / procedures — ways of doing things that have been replaced
  • outdated laws / regulations / policies — rules made for a different time
  • outdated ideas / beliefs / views / thinking — concepts that no longer hold up
  • outdated design / interface / look — visual styles that no longer feel current
  • become outdated / grow outdated — to describe the process of falling behind over time
  • quickly outdated / rapidly outdated — used when something loses currency very fast (e.g., technology)

The natural opposites of "outdated" are:

  • Current — reflects the present moment
  • Up-to-date — has been updated to match the present
  • Modern — belongs to or suits the present era
  • Relevant — applies meaningfully to the present situation
  • Contemporary — existing or occurring in the same time as now

These are designed to show the word in real, natural use:

  1. "The company's website looks outdated — it hasn't been redesigned since 2005."
  2. "Her research is built on outdated data; the figures she's using are from fifteen years ago."
  3. "That approach to teaching is outdated; modern educators now know that memorisation alone isn't effective."
  4. "The GPS in his old car was so outdated that it was still showing roads that had been demolished years ago."
  5. "Some of the safety rules in this factory are outdated and need to be revised."
  6. "He held some outdated views on gender roles that made conversations awkward."
  7. "The phone wasn't broken — it was simply outdated, unable to run any of the newer apps."

Imagine a calendar on a wall. The year shown is 2010. The calendar is perfectly intact — not damaged, not wrong in its own terms. But it is outdated because it no longer tells you anything useful about today. It served its purpose then. It doesn't now.

That gap — between what was once right and what is needed now — is the heart of "outdated."
11523:
To outdo someone means to do something better than they did — to surpass them in performance, quality, achievement, or effort. When you outdo someone, you do not merely match them; you go beyond what they accomplished. The key idea is always doing something at a higher level than someone else.

Imagine two painters competing for a prize: one produces a technically brilliant, emotionally powerful canvas; the other produces something solid but unremarkable. The first painter has outdone the second. The gap matters — "outdo" implies a clear, noticeable difference, not a barely-there victory.
How It Works in a Sentence

"Outdo" is a transitive verb, which means it always needs a direct object — someone or something being surpassed. You cannot say "she outdid" alone; you must specify who or what she outdid.

The structure is: [Person/Thing A] + outdo + [Person/Thing B].

She outdid all her classmates in the science competition.
The small startup outdid its much larger rivals by delivering superior customer service.
His second album outdid his first in both depth and originality.

"Outdo" can also appear in the passive voice, using the past participle "outdone." When someone is outdone, they have been surpassed by another.

She was outdone by a far younger competitor — something nobody had expected.
He refused to be outdone and immediately came back with an even better offer.

"Outdo" is an irregular verb — it does not simply add "-ed" in the past tense. Here is how it changes across tenses.

In the present tense, it is "outdo" for most subjects (I outdo, you outdo, we outdo, they outdo) but changes to "outdoes" when the subject is he, she, or it. In the past tense, it becomes "outdid." The past participle is "outdone," which is used after helping verbs like "have," "has," and "had." The present participle is "outdoing."

She outdoes her brother in every test. (present)
He outdid the champion last night. (past)
She has outdone herself with this performance. (present perfect)
They were outdoing each other to win the contract. (past continuous)

One of the most common and important uses of "outdo" is the phrase "outdo oneself." It means to perform even better than your own previous standard — to surpass your personal best.

This is almost always used as a sincere compliment, saying that someone has done something impressively well — better than what is normally expected of them.

The chef outdid himself with tonight's dinner — it was the finest meal I have ever tasted.
She outdid herself with that speech; the entire room was on its feet.

Occasionally, the same phrase is used sarcastically, to say that someone has made an impressively bad mistake — one that is even worse than their usual standard.

"Well, you've truly outdone yourself this time," said with a sigh after a particularly costly blunder.

Another very common fixed expression is "not to be outdone." It describes someone who refuses to appear inferior or be left behind, and it introduces the action that person takes in response to someone else's impressive move.

He brought flowers to the party. Not to be outdone, she arrived with an entire elaborate gift basket.
The rival company launched a new product. Not to be outdone, the original company immediately announced a better one.

"Outdo" generally implies a meaningful, noticeable level of surpassing — not a razor-thin margin, but a step clearly ahead. In terms of register, it sits comfortably between formal and informal. It sounds natural in casual conversation and is equally at home in professional or academic writing. It carries no negative connotation on its own; it simply acknowledges that something was done at a higher level than something else.

"Outdo" is used in competitive contexts (sport, business, academics), creative contexts (art, writing, film, music), personal and social contexts (generosity, hosting, gift-giving), and in any situation where one party goes a step further than another.

Each new film in the franchise tried to outdo the previous one with larger, louder spectacle.
The two neighbours were always trying to outdo each other with their holiday decorations.
Students were constantly outdoing one another to earn the teacher's praise.

"Outdo" is not the same word as "undo," which means to reverse or cancel something — a completely different meaning. It does not mean to deceive or trick someone. Most importantly, it does not simply mean to try hard or compete — it specifically means to succeed in being better. Someone who gives their best effort but still falls short has not outdone the other person, even if they came close.

Several words share a similar meaning, but each has its own flavour.

"Surpass" means the same thing as "outdo" but is slightly more formal, more often preferred in written English than in casual speech.

"Beat" is more casual and general. While "outdo" focuses on performing better in quality or achievement, "beat" works in a wider range of situations — you beat someone in a game, beat a deadline, or beat an obstacle — contexts where "outdo" would feel unnatural.

"Exceed" focuses on going beyond a set limit, standard, or expectation rather than directly comparing two people. You exceed a target; you outdo a competitor.

"Outperform" is more formal and professional, common in business and finance. It carries the same core meaning but sounds more technical and less personal.

"Top" is informal and means to do better than a previous achievement. "Can anyone top that?" means simply "Can anyone do better?"

Among all these, "outdo" is the most balanced — natural in both everyday talk and formal writing, and most precisely used when one person or thing is being directly compared to and shown to be better than another.
11524:
The word outfit at its heart means a complete set of things that belong together. Whether it's clothes, equipment, or even people — an outfit is never just one thing. It's a collection that forms a whole.

This core idea of completeness and belonging together runs through every meaning of the word.
Meaning 1: A Set of Clothes Worn Together

This is the most common meaning today.

An outfit is a combination of clothing items — and sometimes accessories — that a person wears together at one time, usually chosen to go well with each other.

The key word is together. A single shirt is not an outfit. A single pair of jeans is not an outfit. But a shirt + jeans + shoes + a belt, all worn at the same time as a coordinated look — that is an outfit.

Examples:

  • "She wore a stunning outfit to the wedding — a silk blouse, wide-leg trousers, and gold heels."
  • "I need to pick an outfit for the job interview."
  • "He threw together a casual outfit: a white T-shirt, blue jeans, and sneakers."

What it usually includes:

An outfit typically includes:

  • The main clothing items (shirt, trousers/skirt/dress, jacket)
  • Footwear (shoes, boots, sandals)
  • Sometimes accessories (a bag, a hat, a belt, jewellery)

An outfit is usually put together for a specific occasion or purpose. People speak of a "work outfit," a "gym outfit," a "party outfit," a "travel outfit," and so on. The occasion shapes what the outfit looks like.

The idea of a "complete look":

When someone says they have a great outfit, they mean their clothing works together as a whole. The pieces complement each other — in colour, style, and occasion. An outfit that works well is often described as "put-together" or "polished." One that doesn't is called "mismatched."

This is also why people say things like:

  • "I can't find anything to wear — I don't have a single decent outfit." (She has plenty of clothes, but nothing that comes together as a coherent look.)
  • "That outfit is perfect for the occasion." (The combination of clothes is just right.)

Common expressions:

  • "Put together an outfit" — to choose and assemble the clothing items you'll wear
  • "Wear an outfit" — to have that combination of clothes on your body
  • "Pull off an outfit" — to wear a bold or unusual outfit confidently and successfully
  • "Outfit of the day" (often abbreviated as OOTD) — a popular phrase on social media where people share what they're wearing that day
Meaning 2: A Complete Set of Equipment or Supplies

In this meaning, an outfit is a full set of tools, gear, or equipment that someone needs to do a particular job or activity.

Just like a clothing outfit, this is a collection of things that work together for a specific purpose.

Examples:

  • "He bought a complete camping outfit — a tent, sleeping bag, lantern, and cooking gear."
  • "The soldiers carried their full outfit of equipment into battle."
  • "A plumber's outfit includes wrenches, pipe cutters, sealant tape, and more."

The emphasis here is on completeness. An outfit gives you everything you need — not just one or two items, but the whole set required for the task.

This meaning is somewhat older and less common in everyday conversation today, but you'll still encounter it, especially in historical texts, military contexts, and descriptions of professional trades or outdoor activities.

In informal English, especially American English, outfit can refer to a group of people working together — such as a company, a military unit, a gang, or any organised group.

Examples:

  • "He works for a small tech outfit in Bengaluru." (a small technology company)
  • "The soldiers all belonged to the same outfit." (the same military unit)
  • "That outfit has been running scams for years." (that criminal group/gang)
  • "It's a family-run outfit — the father, mother, and three children all work together."

Why does "outfit" mean a group? The connection comes from Meaning 2. A military unit or a company is, in a sense, a complete set of people equipped and organised for a mission or purpose — just like an outfit of equipment. Over time, this extended naturally to refer to the group itself.

This meaning is casual and informal. You would not use it in formal writing. But in everyday speech, it's a very natural way to refer to a company or group, especially a smaller or tighter-knit one.

What it isExamples
ClothesA complete, coordinated set of clothing itemsA party outfit, a work outfit
EquipmentA complete set of tools or gear for a taskA camping outfit, a soldier's outfit
GroupA complete, organised group of peopleA military outfit, a business outfit

In all three, the word outfit signals: "This is a complete, organised whole — not just a single part."

• Outfit is a countable noun. This means it can be singular or plural.
    • "She has a beautiful outfit."
    • "She has five outfits for the trip."
  • You use the indefinite article "an" before it: "an outfit" (not "a outfit," because "outfit" starts with a vowel sound).
  • The most natural verb to use with it is "wear" (for clothes) or "have" / "own": "She wore a lovely outfit." / "I don't have an outfit for the occasion."

Outfit (noun) has three main meanings:

  1. A set of clothes worn together — the most common, everyday meaning. It refers to a coordinated combination of clothing items (and accessories) chosen for a specific occasion. The whole look together, not a single piece.
  2. A complete set of equipment — all the tools, gear, or supplies needed for a particular job or activity. Emphasises completeness.
  3. A group or organisation (informal) — a company, military unit, or any organised group of people working together.

All three meanings share the same soul: a complete, organised set of things (or people) that work together as a whole.
11525:
To outflank someone means to go around their side in order to gain an advantage over them — whether on a real battlefield or in any competitive situation in life.

The key idea is this: instead of attacking or confronting someone directly from the front, you move cleverly around their side so that you end up in a stronger position than them. It always involves strategy, movement, and outsmarting someone.

The word contains the word "flank" within it. The flank of anything — an army, an animal, a building — simply means its side. Your flanks are your sides, the areas to your left and right.

So "out-flank" = to go beyond someone's flank = to get around their side and past them.

This word was born on the battlefield, and understanding this image will lock the meaning in your mind forever.

Imagine two armies facing each other. Army A is on one side, Army B is on the other. Both armies are prepared to defend against a frontal attack — a straight-on charge from the enemy directly in front of them. Their shields, their guns, their strongest soldiers — all facing forward.

Now, Army A decides not to attack from the front. Instead, they quietly send a large group of soldiers around the side of Army B, curving around them. Suddenly, Army B finds enemy soldiers attacking them from the side or even from behind — directions they weren't prepared for. They are now surrounded, confused, and vulnerable.

Army A has just outflanked Army B.

This was one of the most effective and feared tactics in military history. Generals like Alexander the Great and Napoleon built entire reputations on outflanking their enemies.

Example:

"The general outflanked the enemy by sending his cavalry through the forest to attack from the rear."

Today, most people use "outflank" outside of war entirely. It has moved into business, politics, arguments, sports, and everyday competition. The military image transfers perfectly: instead of going around a physical army, you go around someone's position, strategy, or defense in a clever, non-direct way.

The feeling of the word is always the same:

  • Someone has a defensive position — a plan, an argument, a strategy, a stronghold.
  • Instead of confronting it head-on (which may fail), you find a way around it.
  • You end up in a position of advantage that they didn't see coming.

In politics:

"The opposition party outflanked the government by winning the support of rural voters the government had ignored."

The government thought they were safe. The opposition didn't attack them where they were strong — they went around to an area that wasn't being defended.

In business:

"The startup outflanked its larger rival by targeting a younger audience the rival had overlooked."

Instead of competing directly in the same market (a fight they'd lose), the startup went around to a less-defended market and won.

In a debate or argument:

"She outflanked his argument by bringing up a fact he had never considered."

He thought he had a strong position. She didn't argue against his main point directly — she came at him from a surprising angle that exposed a weakness.

In sports:

"The winger outflanked the defender by sprinting along the edge of the field."

Instead of going through the defender, she went around him on the outside.

Several words might seem similar — like bypass, circumvent, or outmaneuver — but "outflank" carries specific qualities that make it unique:

1. It's competitive. You don't "outflank" an empty room. There is always an opponent involved — someone you are trying to beat or overcome.

2. It implies cleverness and strategy. Outflanking is never accidental. It suggests that you thought about your opponent's position carefully, found a gap or a weak side, and deliberately exploited it. It's a smart move, not a brute-force one.

3. It implies going around, not through. This is crucial. When you outflank someone, you are specifically avoiding their strongest point and finding a route to the side. You don't overpower them head-on — you outsmart them by choosing a better angle.

4. It results in a position of advantage. Outflanking isn't just about moving sideways — the whole point is that you end up better positioned than your opponent as a result.
The Grammar: How to Use It

"Outflank" is a transitive verb, which means it always needs an object — the person or thing being outflanked.

  • ✅ "She outflanked her competitor." (correct — has an object)
  • ❌ "She outflanked." (incorrect — missing an object)

Common forms:

  • Present: outflank / outflanks → "He outflanks his rivals regularly."
  • Past: outflanked → "They outflanked the opposition."
  • Continuous: outflanking → "She is outflanking their strategy."
The Single Sentence to Remember It

If you had to compress the entire meaning of "outflank" into one mental image, remember this:

Instead of hitting the wall, you go around it — and you end up on the other side while your opponent is still staring at where you used to be.

That is what it means to outflank someone.
11526:
To outfox someone means to defeat them or get the better of them by being smarter and more cunning than they are. It is about winning through your mind — not through strength, luck, or resources.

The image behind the word is the fox — an animal long celebrated in stories and culture as a symbol of slyness and clever thinking. When you outfox someone, you are, in spirit, "out-fox-ing" them: you are being more sly and mentally sharp than they are, and that is how you beat them.
What Makes it Different from Simply "Winning"?

Outfoxing is a specific kind of winning. Not every victory counts. To truly outfox someone, three things must be present:

  • A rival — there is always a person (or group, or system) on the other side. You cannot outfox a math problem. You outfox another thinking being.
  • Cleverness or cunning — you thought of something they did not. You were mentally sharper.
  • Strategy or maneuvering — you planned ahead, anticipated their moves, or set a trap.

Without all three, you are not outfoxing — you are simply winning or defeating.

The word carries a slightly sly, crafty quality — this is important. Outfoxing is not just about being book-smart or knowledgeable. It is about thinking in a clever, strategic, sometimes deceptive way. Common ways someone outfoxes another:

  • Predicting what the rival will do before they do it, and using that against them.
  • Making the rival believe something false, so they walk into a trap.
  • Hiding your true plan until it is too late for them to respond.
  • Appearing weak or uninterested, only to strike at the perfect moment.

The element of "getting inside the other person's head" is almost always present.

• It is not about being stronger or more powerful.
  • It is not about having more money or more people on your side.
  • It is not about being lucky.
  • It is not a straightforward, fair-and-square contest of skill. There is always a clever angle — a bit of craftiness involved.

If a boxer beats another boxer simply because they are stronger, that is not outfoxing. But if a smaller, weaker boxer wins by studying the opponent's habits, predicting every punch, and staying one step ahead mentally — that is outfoxing.

Here are varied examples to help you feel the word in action:

  1. The detective outfoxed the thief by pretending to leave town, then quietly returned and caught him red-handed.
  2. The small startup outfoxed its giant rival by launching quietly and capturing the market before anyone noticed.
  3. She outfoxed the entire negotiating team by making them believe she was desperate for the deal, when in reality, she had a better offer waiting.
  4. The chess grandmaster outfoxed his opponent with a move no one had anticipated.
  5. The rabbit outfoxed the fox by doubling back through its own footprints, confusing the trail.
  6. Despite having fewer resources, the general outfoxed the enemy army by striking from an unexpected direction.

Notice: in every sentence, someone clever beats someone else through thinking, strategy, or cunning — never through brute force alone.
How Outfox Compares to Similar Words

These words are related but not identical:

  • Outsmart — the closest synonym. To beat someone using intelligence. Slightly more neutral and broader than outfox. Outfox has a stronger flavor of cunning and slyness; outsmart can simply mean "to be smarter."
  • Outwit — also very close. Emphasizes mental speed and sharpness of thinking in the moment. Outfox leans more toward planned, crafty strategy; outwit can be a quicker, more spontaneous flash of cleverness.
  • Outmaneuver — to beat someone through better tactical moves, often implying physical or strategic positioning (in battle, negotiation, competition). Less emphasis on deception than outfox.
  • Trick or deceive — simpler words, but they miss the competitive element. You can trick someone without there being a battle of wits. Outfox always implies a contest.

In short: outfox is the most vivid and colorful of these words, with the strongest sense of sly, cunning intelligence winning over a genuine opponent.
Tone and Register: When and Where to Use It

"Outfox" sits comfortably in everyday, informal to semi-formal English. It has a slightly playful, vivid quality — it brings color to a sentence. You will commonly find it in:

  • Casual conversation: "She totally outfoxed him in that argument."
  • News and journalism (especially business, politics, sports): "The opposition outfoxed the ruling party with a surprise announcement."
  • Storytelling and narratives.

It is not a slang word — it is perfectly respectable. However, it is too colorful for cold, formal academic writing, where you would instead write something like "outmaneuver" or "circumvent."
Grammar: How to Build a Sentence with It

"Outfox" is a transitive verb, which means it always needs an object — someone who is being outfoxed. You cannot simply say "she outfoxed" and stop there. You must say who was outfoxed.

Pattern: Subject + outfoxed + object

✅ Correct❌ Incorrect
"She outfoxed him.""She outfoxed."
"They outfoxed the entire system.""They outfoxed."

It works in all tenses:

  • Present: He outfoxes his competitors at every turn.
  • Past: She outfoxed the lawyer in the courtroom.
  • Future: They will outfox the enemy before the week is over.
  • Continuous: The spy is outfoxing the entire agency, one step at a time.
  • Passive voice: The experienced negotiator was outfoxed by the young newcomer. (Here, the subject is on the losing end.)

The passive voice form ("was outfoxed") is quite common and useful when you want to highlight the person who lost the battle of wits.
One-Line Summary to Anchor It All
To outfox someone = to beat them by being more clever and cunning than they are, using strategy, smart thinking, or slyness — not strength or luck.
11527: "Outgoing" has two separate meanings as an adjective, and they are quite different from each other. You need to know both to truly understand this word.

This is the most common and important meaning. When you describe a person as outgoing, you mean they are naturally comfortable and enthusiastic around other people. They enjoy socializing, meeting strangers, starting conversations, and being part of a group. Being around others gives them energy rather than draining them.

An outgoing person:

  • walks into a room full of strangers and starts talking without hesitation
  • makes friends easily and quickly
  • is warm, cheerful, and approachable
  • enjoys parties, social gatherings, and group activities
  • speaks up confidently in conversations

This is a personality trait — something stable about how a person is, not just how they behave on one particular day.

Examples:

  • "She is so outgoing — she introduced herself to everyone at the party within minutes."
  • "He's very outgoing, which makes him excellent at his job as a salesperson."
  • "Even as a child, Maya was outgoing and never afraid to raise her hand in class."

What "outgoing" does NOT mean here

Being outgoing does not mean being loud, rude, or overbearing. An outgoing person can be perfectly polite and respectful — they are simply at ease with social interaction. It also doesn't mean they have no depth or are shallow. Many thoughtful, intelligent people are outgoing.

It also does not mean the same as being extroverted in the clinical, psychological sense, though the two words are very closely related and are often used interchangeably in everyday speech. In casual use, saying someone is "outgoing" or "extroverted" usually means the same thing.

The scale of outgoing-ness

"Outgoing" is not all-or-nothing. People can be:

  • Very outgoing — the life of the party, loves being the center of attention
  • Fairly outgoing — comfortable in social situations but doesn't need to be the loudest person in the room
  • Somewhat outgoing — can socialize well when needed but doesn't actively seek it out

Synonyms and how they differ

  • Sociable — very similar; means enjoying the company of others. Perhaps slightly softer than "outgoing." An outgoing person is always sociable, but a sociable person isn't always as bold or as energetic about it as an outgoing person.
  • Extroverted — nearly identical in everyday use. In psychology, an extrovert is someone who gains energy from social interaction.
  • Friendly — this just means being warm and pleasant toward others. A friendly person might still be shy or reserved. Outgoing goes further — it also implies actively seeking social connection.
  • Gregarious — very similar to outgoing, but slightly more formal. It specifically emphasizes enjoying group settings and the company of many people.
  • Confident — being outgoing usually involves confidence, but confidence is broader (you can be confident about many things). An outgoing person has social confidence specifically.

Antonym

The opposite of outgoing (in this sense) is introverted, reserved, shy, or withdrawn.

  • Shy — feels nervous, uncomfortable, or self-conscious around others
  • Reserved — not shy necessarily, but keeps to themselves, doesn't open up easily
  • Introverted — prefers less social stimulation; socializing feels draining rather than energizing
Meaning 2: Leaving, Departing, or Going Out

This is the second meaning, used in very specific, mostly formal or official contexts. Here, "outgoing" simply means something that is in the process of leaving or going out, as opposed to coming in.

Examples:

  • "The outgoing president" — the president who is currently finishing their term and about to leave the position (as opposed to the incoming president who is just taking over)
  • "Outgoing mail" — letters or packages being sent out from an office (as opposed to incoming mail, which is being received)
  • "The outgoing tide" — the tide that is currently moving away from the shore (as opposed to the incoming tide)
  • "The outgoing flight" — a flight that is departing (especially when seen from the perspective of the place it's leaving)

Notice that in this meaning, "outgoing" is almost always paired with a noun — it describes that noun as "going out" or "leaving." This meaning is fairly straightforward and you will almost always understand it from the context.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

Context will always make it clear:

  • If "outgoing" describes a person's character or personality, it means sociable and friendly.
  • If "outgoing" describes a position, a message, a tide, or something leaving, it means departing or going out.

You will almost never confuse the two in real life.
A Note on Register and Usage

In its personality sense, "outgoing" is a positive and complimentary word. Calling someone outgoing is generally a compliment — it suggests they are easy to be around and fun in social settings. It is used equally in casual conversation and professional writing. You might see it on a resume ("I am an outgoing team player"), in a novel describing a character, or in everyday speech about someone you know.

In its departing sense, "outgoing" tends to appear in formal or institutional language — official documents, news articles, business communication, and so on. It is less common in casual, everyday speech.

Outgoing (about a person): Naturally sociable, friendly, comfortable meeting new people, and energized by social interaction.

Outgoing (about things/positions): Currently leaving, being sent out, or in the final phase before being replaced — the opposite of "incoming."
11528:
To outgross something or someone means to earn more money in total revenue than another thing or person, typically in a competition or comparison.

The key word buried inside it is "gross," which in financial language simply means the total amount of money earned before any expenses, taxes, or deductions are taken out. Think of it as the raw, full number on the scoreboard — every dollar that came in, counted together.

The prefix "out-" means to beat, surpass, or do better than someone else in a specific way. You already know this from everyday words like outrun (run faster than), outsmart (be smarter than), or outlast (last longer than).

So put them together: outgross = to earn a higher gross revenue than someone or something else.

This word appears most heavily in the film and entertainment industry, where movies are constantly being compared by how much money they made at the box office (the total ticket sales worldwide or domestically).

"Avatar outgrossed Titanic to become the highest-earning film of all time."

This means Avatar pulled in more total ticket revenue than Titanic did.

"The sequel outgrossed the original by nearly $200 million."

The sequel earned $200 million more in total than the first film.

You'll also see it in business and finance more broadly:

"Company A outgrossed Company B in the second quarter."

Company A brought in more total revenue than Company B during that period.

Imagine two lemonade stands in your neighborhood. At the end of the week, Stand A collected $300 in sales and Stand B collected $180.

Stand A outgrossed Stand B. It doesn't matter what they spent on lemons, cups, or sugar — those are expenses, and gross doesn't care about expenses. Gross is only about what came in. Stand A simply brought in more money.

1. Gross ≠ Profit.
This is critical. Outgrossing something does not automatically mean being more profitable. A film can outgross another film in ticket sales and still lose money if it cost far more to make. Outgross is purely about the top-line number — total revenue collected — not what's left over after costs.

Example: Film X earned $500 million (cost $450 million to make). Film Y earned $300 million (cost $80 million to make). Film X outgrossed Film Y — but Film Y was actually more profitable.

2. The comparison is always relative.
You always outgross something — a rival, a predecessor, a record. The word implies a head-to-head comparison. You wouldn't say "this film outgrossed" and stop there; it needs an opponent or a benchmark to beat.

3. It's a transitive verb.
This means it always needs an object — something being outgrossed. You outgross a film, a competitor, a record, a rival company.

ConceptExplanation

Outgross means to exceed another entity in gross (total) earnings. It's used when comparing revenue figures between two things — usually films, companies, or products. It says nothing about profit, only about which one brought in more money altogether. The winner of that comparison is said to have outgrossed the other.
11529:
The word outgrow is built from two parts: out + grow. When you put "out-" before a verb, it usually means to go beyond or to surpass. So outgrow means to grow beyond something — to reach a point where something no longer fits you, suits you, or is enough for you anymore, because you have grown.

The key idea is always a gap: you were once the right size for something — physically, mentally, or emotionally — and then you grew, and now there's a mismatch. That thing got "left behind."

Meaning 1: To become physically too large for something

This is the most literal and easiest meaning. A person (usually a child) grows in body size until something no longer fits them.

"My son outgrew his shoes in just three months."

This means his feet grew so much that the shoes became too small for him.

"She outgrew her bicycle and needed a bigger one."

Notice: it is not the shoes or the bicycle that changed. He grew. She grew. The object stayed the same — the person surpassed it in size.

This meaning is almost always about children growing physically, though it can sometimes apply to animals or even objects (a plant outgrowing its pot, for example).

Meaning 2: To mature past something — to no longer need, enjoy, or be suited to something

This is the most important and widely used meaning. Here, the "growing" is not physical — it is mental, emotional, or personal. As a person matures, develops, and gains experience, they sometimes find that certain things from their past no longer fit who they are now.

Think of it like this: just as a shoe can become too small for a growing foot, an old habit, fear, interest, or relationship can become "too small" for a growing mind or personality.

Examples:

"He used to be very shy, but he outgrew it."

He was shy before. Over time, as he matured and gained confidence, the shyness stopped being a part of him. He grew beyond it.

"She outgrew her fear of the dark."

As a child, she was afraid. As she got older and her understanding of the world developed, the fear faded away naturally.

"They were best friends in school, but they outgrew each other."

Their personalities, interests, and life paths changed as they matured. What once connected them was no longer enough. Neither person is "bad" — they simply grew in different directions.

"I used to love cartoon shows, but I outgrew them."

As you get older, your tastes change. The things that once excited you may no longer match who you are.

Important nuance: When you outgrow something in this sense, there is usually no blame and no regret attached to it. It is a natural, often positive process. You didn't reject it — you simply grew beyond it. This is what makes "outgrow" different from words like "abandon" or "quit." Outgrowing happens gradually and naturally, as a consequence of personal growth.

Meaning 3: To grow faster or larger than something else

This meaning is commonly used in professional or organizational contexts. It means that something (a company, a city, a system) grows at such a fast pace that it exceeds the capacity or size of something that was meant to contain or support it.

"The startup outgrew its small office and had to move to a bigger building."

The company expanded so rapidly that the office space was no longer sufficient.

"The city has outgrown its water supply."

The population grew so large that the existing water infrastructure can no longer meet its needs.

"The project outgrew its original budget."

The project expanded beyond what the budget was designed to cover.

Here, the subject is not a person but an organization, system, or place — and it grows beyond the limits of something else.

Here are the most natural and common things people say you can outgrow:

Physical things:
clothes, shoes, a crib, a car seat, a bedroom, a bicycle

Habits and behaviors:
a bad habit, shyness, a temper, clumsiness, nail-biting

Fears and feelings:
a fear, an insecurity, jealousy, anxiety about something specific

Interests and hobbies:
a TV show, a music genre, a game, a type of book

Relationships and social connections:
a friendship, a relationship, a community, a mentor

Roles, places, and situations:
a job, a school, a city, a company, a stage of life

Systems and structures (organizational):
an office, a platform, a system, a budget, a market

Outgrow is a transitive verb — it always takes an object. You outgrow something. You cannot just say "He outgrew" and leave it there. You must say what was outgrown.

Forms:

  • Present: outgrow / outgrows
  • Past simple: outgrew
  • Past participle: outgrown
  • Present participle: outgrowing

"Children outgrow their clothes quickly."
"She outgrew her fear as she got older." (past simple)
"He has outgrown that phase completely." (past participle with "have")
"The company is outgrowing its current space." (present participle / continuous)
The Subtle Emotion Behind the Word

One beautiful thing about "outgrow" is its tone. It is almost always neutral to positive. It suggests natural development, not rejection. When someone says "I outgrew that friendship," they are not saying the friend was bad — they are saying that life moved them in a new direction. When a parent says "She outgrew her clothes," it's almost a proud statement of the child's growth.

However, outgrowing something can sometimes carry a quiet sadness — especially when it involves relationships or beloved parts of your past. You might outgrow a best friend, a hometown, or a dream, and while the growth itself is good, there can be a sense of loss for what is being left behind.

ContextWhat "outgrow" means

In short:

Outgrow means to grow to a point where something — a physical object, a habit, a fear, a relationship, a role, or a system — no longer fits or suits you (or something) because of that growth. The "growing" can be physical (body size), personal (maturity, taste, personality), or organizational (scale, capacity). In every case, the core idea is the same: growth has created a gap between where you are now and where something else remains.
